title: Masculine, feminine, and the table
goal: Build the habit that shapes the rest of the course: every noun has a gender, and its article and adjectives must follow along. Plus: making plurals.
bekal: choose *o* or *a* for a new noun by guessing from its ending
make plurals with *-s* and switch the article to *os* / *as*
put the adjective **after** the noun and match its ending

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Na livraria
dialogs.intro: Budi is looking for a book in a small bookstore on Rua Augusta. A shop assistant comes over.

lines.speaker: Vendedor:
lines.id: Good afternoon! Can I help you?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Boa tarde. Eu procuro um livro de português.
lines.id: Good afternoon. I'm looking for a Portuguese book.
lines.literal: good afternoon. I I-look-for a book of Portuguese.

lines.speaker: Vendedor:
lines.text: Claro. O livro é para você?
lines.id: Sure. Is the book for you?
lines.literal: clear. the book is for you?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Yes, it is. I'm a student.

lines.speaker: Vendedor:
lines.text: Temos uma gramática nova e um dicionário pequeno.
lines.id: We have a new grammar book and a small dictionary.
lines.literal: we-have a grammar new and a dictionary small.

lines.speaker: Vendedor:
lines.text: É excelente. E os exercícios são fáceis.
lines.id: It's excellent. And the exercises are easy.
lines.literal: is excellent. and the(pl) exercises are easy(pl).

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: E as fotos? O livro tem fotos?

lines.literal: and the(pl) photos? the book it-has photos?

lines.speaker: Vendedor:
lines.text: Tem, sim. As páginas são bem coloridas.

lines.literal: it-has, yes. the(pl) pages are well colorful(pl).

notes: **Every thing has a gender, even things that obviously don't.** *O livro* (book) is masculine; *a mesa* (table) is feminine. There's no logical reason, and hunting for one is a waste of time. What you can rely on isn't the meaning but **the ending of the word** — and that works for about eight words out of ten.

**Adjectives come after the noun.** *um livro pequeno* = "a book small", *uma gramática nova* = "a grammar new". It's the reverse of English, and English speakers spend months fighting the urge to write *um pequeno livro*. Read the dialogue aloud a few times and the right order starts to sound natural.

**And the adjective changes too.** This part has no equivalent in English: *livro pequen**o***, but *mesa pequen**a***; *livros pequen**os***, *mesas pequen**as***. The adjective copies the gender and number of its noun, like a shadow.

**Bem coloridas, not muito coloridas.** *Bem* before an adjective means "quite/really", and in Brazil it's heard far more often than *muito* in casual conversation. *A comida é bem gostosa* = "the food is really tasty".

grammars.title: Articles: four definite, four indefinite
body: English has just *the* and *a/an*; Portuguese has a form for every gender and number. The good news: the whole table is only eight words, and they're among the most frequent in Portuguese, so they stick on their own.
after: **The definite article is used far more often than you'd expect.** Portuguese puts it in front of things that stand bare in English: *o Brasil* (Brazil), *a vida* (life), *o português* (Portuguese), even *a Carla* (a person's name). Rough rule: when in doubt, put it in.
*Uns* and *umas* mean "some": *uns livros* = some books. They're used less often than the other forms.

⚠️ Memorizing nouns without their article is the most expensive mistake of your whole learning journey, because fixing it later means relearning every word from scratch. Write **o livro**, not *livro*. Always.

grammars.title: Guessing gender from the ending
body: Eight out of ten nouns follow the rules below. The rest are learned one by one, and there are fewer of them than you fear.
after: ⚠️ Four exceptions you must learn because they're so common: **o dia** (day) is masculine even though it ends in -a; **o problema**, **o mapa** and **o programa** are masculine too. Most come from Greek, and they all misbehave the same way.

Words for people follow the person's gender, and usually have two forms: *o professor / a professora*, *o amigo / a amiga*, *o brasileiro / a brasileira*. Some have a single form for both, and only the article changes: *o estudante / a estudante*, *o dentista / a dentista*.

grammars.title: Plurals: add -s
body: The basic rule is as simple as in English, and four extra lines cover the rest.
after: **Everything attached goes plural too.** If the noun is plural, its article and adjective are plural as well: *as casas bonitas* — three words, three *s*'s. English marks the plural once (*the beautiful houses*); Portuguese marks it on every word in the chain.

⚠️ The last row has two stubborn groups: *o pão* → *os pães* (bread) and *a mão* → *as mãos* (hand). All three patterns *-ões*, *-ães*, *-ãos* exist; *-ões* is by far the most common, and the other two are simply learned when you meet them.

blocks.text: Learn this table **together with the articles**. Never say a word from the first column without the little word in front of it.

Note *a água* (water): a feminine word that starts with a stressed **a**. Some languages change the article here (Spanish says *el agua*); Portuguese doesn't. It stays *a água*, and the plural is *as águas*.
Portuguese adjectives come in two groups. Those ending in **-o** have four forms; those ending in **-e** or a consonant change only for the plural.

The last three rows are good news: *grande*, *fácil*, *difícil* (and *feliz*) **don't care** whether the noun is masculine or feminine. *Um livro grande*, *uma casa grande* — exactly the same. About a third of Portuguese adjectives behave this way.

⚠️ *Bom* is both the most irregular adjective and the most used. Notice that its feminine form isn't *boma* but **boa** — and that's where *boa tarde* and *boa noite* from unit 1 come from, while masculine *dia* gets *bom dia*.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the blanks with the right definite article: o, a, os or as.
Make it plural. Write out the whole phrase.

answers: O — A — Os — As — O — A
